# A full-dimensional nested simplex mixture need not have depth Gamma

Let T=conv(0,e_1,e_2), let delta=1/100, and let mu_R denote normalized
uniform area on a positive-area convex set R. The probability measure

    nu=(1/5)mu_(delta T)+(4/5)mu_T                  (1)

has compact convex support T, is a mixture of only two nested common-
vertex homothetic simplex laws, and is absolutely continuous. Nevertheless

    max_y depth_nu(y)
      <=(77-16 sqrt(13))/45 <4/9.                  (2)

This is an obstruction to a proposed transport-target inheritance rule.
It is not an OC counterexample: nu is not uniform area on T or mixed
integer volume on a convex-body intersection.

## 1. Symmetry reduces the upper-bound candidates rigorously

The law is invariant under exchange of the two coordinates. Halfspace
depth has convex superlevel sets: if several points have depth at least
a, any halfspace containing a convex combination of them contains at
least one of those points and consequently has mass at least a. Thus
averaging a point with its coordinate exchange cannot decrease depth.

Any point outside T has depth zero by strict separation. It therefore
suffices for an upper bound on the global maximum to consider points
y=(t,t) with 0<=t<=1/2. This does not restrict normal directions: for
an upper bound it suffices to exhibit actual containing caps at each
such candidate. All boundaries have nu-mass zero, including those
passing through vertices of the small simplex.

## 2. Two exact caps cover the entire diagonal

For 0<=t<=delta, the cap H_-={x_1+x_2<=2t} contains y. Its mass is
at most

    1/5+(4/5)(2delta)^2=1/5+(16/5)delta^2.        (3)

The inner component contributes at most its entire weight. The outer
component's lower triangular cap has fraction(2t)^2, since2delta<1.

For delta<=t<=1/2 the cap H_+={x_1>=t} contains y and its small-
simplex contribution is zero. At t=delta this is still true because
the intersection in that component is just a vertex. Thus

    nu(H_+)=(4/5)(1-t)^2.                         (4)

In this range H_- contains the entire small simplex, since its maximum
coordinate sum is delta<=2t. Hence

    nu(H_-)=1/5+(16/5)t^2.                        (5)

The expression in (4) decreases and that in (5) increases on this
interval. They are equal at the unique positive solution

    t_*=(sqrt(13)-2)/6,
    3t_*^2+2t_*-3/4=0.                           (6)

The elementary inequalities3<sqrt(13)<4 put t_* in(1/6,1/3), hence
strictly between delta and1/2. Their maximum possible minimum is

    (4/5)(1-t_*)^2=(77-16 sqrt(13))/45.            (7)

The bound(3) is strictly smaller than13/45, while (7) exceeds13/45
because sqrt(13)<4. Thus (3)-(7) prove the global upper bound in (2).
No claim that these two caps alone give the exact maximum is needed.

Finally (7)<4/9 is equivalent to57<16 sqrt(13). Both sides are
positive, and squaring gives the exact strict inequality

    57^2=3249 <3328=16^2*13.                      (8)

This is a strict positive-area example; no singular point-mass limit,
open-halfspace substitution, or approximate numerical optimization
is involved.

## 3. Consequence for radial pairing proposals

Coupling two common-vertex simplex fibers by the same normalized angular
point creates another common-vertex simplex law; mixtures over many
pairing choices can therefore create nested laws of the form(1).
It is not valid to infer depth at least Gamma merely from that nested
mixture description or from radial decrease of the resulting density.
A successful pairing theorem must retain further constraints imposed
by the actual source and the shared ambient tilt, or prove a stronger
property of its particular target law. This note makes no assertion
that the specific mixture(1) is forced by an actual concave radius chain.
